labyrinth

/LAB-uh-rinth/ — rhymes with hint · noun

Hear It

What It Means

A labyrinth is a complicated network of winding passages that is easy to get lost in.

The old palace was a labyrinth of staircases that led visitors in circles.

Example

The castle's interior was such a labyrinth of narrow corridors and hidden chambers that guests relied on printed maps to find their way to the main hall.

Labyrinth emphasizes the confusing, winding nature of the passages and how easy it is to get lost. While 'maze' is similar, a maze is deliberately designed to challenge the solver, whereas a labyrinth suggests an older, organically complex structure. Labyrinth carries more grandeur and historical weight.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

maze: A maze is a puzzle of paths built on purpose to challenge whoever enters - corn mazes, puzzle-book mazes - and solving it is the point of the game. A labyrinth is not a game: it is a real place, often old and grand, whose passages grew confusing over time rather than by design.

tangle: A tangle is a confused, twisted mass - knotted string, snarled cables, wet hair - something you pick apart with your fingers, not a place you can enter. A labyrinth is built space: passage after passage that a person walks into, and inside which a person can genuinely get lost.

web: A web is a pattern of threads or links spreading between points - a spider's web, a web of friendships - and you usually see it whole, from the outside, as a design. A labyrinth is experienced from the inside: passages that keep turning a walker around until the way out disappears.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

clarity: the quality of being easily understood

simplicity: plainness that makes something easy to follow

Where it sits · how easily you can get lost

path → network → warren → labyrinth

path vs. labyrinth: A path is the humblest point on this scale compared with a labyrinth: a path leads you plainly from one place to another, while a labyrinth is built to make you lose your way.

network vs. labyrinth: A network is weaker than a labyrinth — a network is an organized web of connections, but a labyrinth is a tangle of winding passages designed to confuse.

warren vs. labyrinth: A warren comes close to a labyrinth, but labyrinth is the stronger word: a warren of cramped hallways can turn a stranger around for a while, while a labyrinth is a grand, elaborate structure that can swallow a walker for hours.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — labyrinth: maze; building of winding passages (Greek labyrinthos) (Greek)

Put it together: The whole word is one ancient root: Greek labyrinthos, the vast building of winding passages in the Cretan myth of the Minotaur — so a labyrinth is any complicated network of paths that is easy to get lost in. (The Greek word's own deeper source is lost; one speculative theory ties it to labrys, a 'double axe' symbol of the Minoan palace.)

Use the root in a new word: labyrinthine: The detective's labyrinthine investigation twisted through false leads for months before it finally reached the truth. Labyrinthine simply puts labyrinth to work as an adjective — Greek labyrinthos, the word for the winding building of legend.

Word Building

Word Choice

formal / literary

Labyrinth describes a genuinely complex, confusing structure—often physical, sometimes figurative. It carries a sense of history and grandeur, suggesting something where you might genuinely get lost. For a simple puzzle game or organized structure, use 'maze' or 'network' instead.
